newsitem.title: USA: Gore, Kemp waltz in scholarly campaign debate.
newsitem.headline: Gore, Kemp waltz in scholarly campaign debate.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore and Republican Jack Kemp debated economic, social and foreign policy on Wednesday like two polite professors on adjoining bar-stools at the faculty club, each mildly annoyed with the other chap's views.

Gore, carrying front-running President Bill Clinton's banner, and Kemp, striving to promote underdog Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole, held a 90-minute televised running-mates debate that showed voters in detail -- lots of detail -- what happens when a well-mannered, brainy conservative meets a well-mannered, brainy middle-roader.

They disagreed on everything, each taking an occasional shot at the other when patience grew strained and leaving voters to take their choice between clear dry alternatives when it comes time to vote on Nov. 5.

Gore's sharpest thrust may have been when he laughed off a claim that Dole's proposal for a sweeping 15 percent tax cut -- the very heart of his campaign -- would create a surging "Niagara Falls" of economic boons for Americans.

"The problem with this version of Niagara Falls is that Senator Dole and Mr. Kemp would put the economy in a barrel and send it over Niagara Falls," said Gore, who portrayed the Dole plan as budget-busting nonsense.
Kemp's strongest swipes tended to be wordier, and a bit more passionate than those of the notoriously bland Gore.
"Al, get real," Kemp barked at one point after Gore suggested Republicans would wreck the environment. "Franklin Roosevelt said in 1932 that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.

"The only thing they (Gore and Clinton) have to offer is fear: Fear of the environment, fear of the climate, fear of Medicare, fear of Newt (Gingrich), fear of Republicans, fear of Bob (Dole), probably fear of cutting tax rates. They ain't seen nothing yet."

Neither made the sort of egregious verbal blunder that has occasionally sunk U.S. campaign debaters in the past, nor did Kemp appear to score the sort of sparkling breakthrough that might have been tonic to his struggling Republican ticket.

That was similar to the result of the first Clinton-Dole debate last Sunday and left the Republicans one last big chance to score before a huge televised audience with the main candidates hold a second debate on Oct. 16.

Gore and Kemp, each an intellectual of some standing on the political issues that interest them, started out all sweetness and light by exchanging promises to keep a high tone to their debate and shun personal attacks.
"Bob Dole and myself do not see Al Gore and Bill Clinton as our enemy, we see them as opponents," said Kemp, nodding at Gore who stood a few feet away behind a pulpit-like lectern.
Although some Republicans have been urging Dole to start attacking Clinton's character and credibility, Kemp said, "It is beneath Bob Dole to go after anyone personally."
Gore expressed gratitude for that sentiment, and added at debates end in sincere tones: "I have enormous respect for Jack Kemp and Bob Dole. They're good men."
They not only shook hands at the end but slapped each other on the back like old pals.
Even so, each man took his pokes at the other when opportunity arose in a scholarly dialogue that focussed heavily on the U.S. tax code and how it should be reformed.

Minutes after his opening bow to Gore, Kemp was asserting that U.S. foreign policy under Clinton "is ambivalent, confusing, it is sending wrong signals to the wrong people, and we've learned ... that weakness is provocative."
Gore scoffed at that, saying Clinton had showed towering leadership in helping bring about peace in Bosnia, democracy in Haiti and a truce however temporary in Northern Ireland.
Gore in turn lampooned the Dole tax-cut proposal as "a risky $550 billion tax scheme that would blow a hole in the (federal) deficit ... and knock our economy off-track."
Much better, he said, was Clinton's more modest counter proposal to offer some tax cuts targeted to the middle-class.
Kemp snorted that the economy under Clinton and Gore "is over-taxed and over-litigated" and that "the only hole (the Dole tax-cut) would blow would be a hole in the plans of this administration."

They outlined the familiar disagreements as well on abortion, on which the Democrats favor choice for women and the Republicans do not, and on affirmative action racial policies in hiring and schools, which the Republicans would repeal and the Democrats would only revise.

Gore insisted the Republicans would have to raid Medicare and Medicaid federal insurance programs for the elderly and poor to finance their tax plan -- a kiss of death among those voting constituencies -- and Kemp insisted Gore was just engaging in "demagogy" and "scaring senior citizens."
After the debate, strategists for each side rushed out to tell reporters their man had won in the "spin" sessions now customary at these affairs.
